text:
When the infant forehead, with its red storms,
calls up the white swarm of vague dreams,
two laughing sisters come to the bedside
with their graceful fingers, silver-nailed.


They seat the child before the open window,
where blue air bathes whirlwinds of flowers,
and through his thick hair, heavy with dew,
their fingers pass, seductive, terrible.


He listens to the song of their timid breaths,
which spread broad honeys of plants and roses
and are sometimes interrupted by a whistle—saliva
the lips draw in, or the desire to kiss.


He hears their eyelashes beat in the perfumed
silence; and their fingers, electric and soft,
bring about, amid gray indolences, the clicks
of dead lice crushed by their queenly nails.


And a wine of Sloth rises in him, a harmonica
sigh capable of reaching delirium:
and the child feels, to the slow rhythm of the caresses,
how his urges to weep are born and die.

translation.title: The Lice-Pickers
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, rather than from Rimbaud's French original. The unsettling tenderness, bodily ambiguity, and stanza structure are preserved.
